extracted.intended_audience: instructors, instructional designers, and administrators planning or implementing online learning (higher education and distance education)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for planning, organizing, and choosing pedagogies, technologies, and governance for online learning systems; includes pedagogical orientations (progressive, behaviourist, humanist, radical, analytical) and infrastructural/organizational considerations for LMS selection and ongoing change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progressive orientation — aims and teacher role
rubrics_metrics.description: The teacher/student relationship is best characterized as a partnership. Learning is something that students do for themselves. Education involves experience, which is reflected and acted upon by the student. The result is knowledge that is inseparable from ever-changing experiences. Learning also involves liberating the learner for the potential improvement of society and culture. In particular, learning is not enough; sooner or later, students must act as a consequence of their learning. The teacher’s role is to organize, stimulate, instigate, and evaluate the highly complex process of education. This can be effectively achieved by being a helper, consultant, and/or encourager. When the teacher provides a setting that is conductive to this form of learning, the teacher also becomes a learner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preferred emphasis on learner-centred activities; use conferencing and asynchronous communication to design interactive partnerships; asynchronous technologies can give students equal opportunities to contribute and create a democratic learning environment. Criticisms: overreliance on education for social change; too much emphasis on student-centredness may underplay teacher role and subject matter importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behaviourist orientation — goals, methods, and role of technology
rubrics_metrics.description: The ultimate goal of the behaviourist orientation is to bring about observable changes in behaviour. Methods of instruction begin with stated learning objectives, accompanied by the inclusion of rewards and punishments toward and away from the stated behavioural objectives. The focus of the learning is on the content, with a subject-centred approach. The role of the teacher is to design an environment that elicits desired behaviour toward meeting these goals and to extinguish behaviour that is not desirable; the teacher is a contingency manager or an environmental controller. Students’ role is active rather than passive; responsibility lies primarily with the student. According to behaviourists, students have learned something if there is a change in behaviour and if their response occurs again under similar circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Behaviourists align with technological determinism: computer-based tutorials and simulations, standardized course management systems, and learning objects are seen as effective and efficient. Course management systems can regulate teacher activities, track students’ activities, provide immediate feedback via assessment tools, and support modularized courses with stated objectives and end-of-unit assessment tools. Criticisms: predetermined behavioural objectives can neglect incidental learning, dehumanize students, inhibit creativity, and fragment curriculum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humanist orientation — aims, teacher role, and technology uses
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary aim of the humanist orientation is to support individual growth and self-actualization. Key constructs include freedom and autonomy, trust, active cooperation and participation, and self-directed learning. The role of the teacher is that of facilitator, helper, and partner in the learning process; the teacher must create conditions within which learning can take place and encourage students to set their own goals. The focus is on the individual student’s growth and development and on affective rather than cognitive aspects of education. Self-evaluation is the only meaningful test of whether learning has taken place (according to humanists).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humanists align most closely with uses determinism: e-learning technologies can provide flexibility, convenience, just-in-time learning, and meet individual needs. Social software and online classrooms can facilitate group relations and discovery; online contexts may make the teacher necessarily a facilitator. Objections include that arbitrary institutional decisions about technologies violate students’ ability to identify their own learning needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Radical orientation — aims, methods, and critique of commercial technologies
rubrics_metrics.description: The overarching aim of the radical perspective is to invoke change in the political, economic, and social order via the intersection of education and political action. Preferred instructional methods are dialogic encounters that lead to praxis (e.g., problem posing, problem identification through dialogue based on respect, communication, and solidarity). The role of the teacher is to raise students’ consciousness of social and political contradictions; participants must be free to create the curriculum along with the teacher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Radicals align with social determinism regarding technology: commercialized products (WebCT, Blackboard, Lotus Notes) are viewed as enforcing a corporate communication paradigm and problematic (e.g., surveillance features). Open-source technologies (e.g., Moodle) are preferable. Criticisms: methods may be impractical in many educational environments (mandatory grading, lack of risk-free spaces); tensions about teachers exercising power when imparting information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytical orientation — aims, instructional methods, and tech role
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary aim of the analytical orientation is the development of rationality, assisted by the fearless transmission of educationally worthwhile knowledge. Dialogue through class discussion, guided and directed by the teacher, is considered the ideal method. Teachers should identify what students do not know and determine aims and objectives; the teacher makes choices about things that are educationally worthwhile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyticals align with uses determinism: e-learning technologies can serve under certain circumstances (e.g., lectures downloadable to web pages and follow-up dialogue facilitated and directed by the teacher using group communication tools). Critics question whether any programmatic decision can truly be neutral or value-free.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match technologies to pedagogical/philosophical orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: When we are aware of our philosophical orientation, it is then possible to make informed decisions about choosing and using e-learning technology. Without knowing our philosophical orientation, other strategies are used (often following the latest trend) leading to incongruence and inconsistency in action between and among instructors, administrators, and students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 'mindless activism' for technology adoption. Ensure congruence between beliefs (pedagogy) and actions (technology choices). Thoughtful practitioners should know not only what they do but why they do it; experience combined with reflection leads to purposeful and informed action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-development stock-taking: learners, curriculum, and context
rubrics_metrics.description: Before embarking on the development of an online learning system, in part or in whole, careful stock needs to be taken of the needs of the intended learners, the curriculum to be offered, and the context for the project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider planning, structural and organizational issues, the components of a system and the interfaces among them, and related issues such as human resources, decision-making, and training. Use knowledge from other chapters/areas (design, development, delivery) to inform infrastructure planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infrastructure must be able to evolve
rubrics_metrics.description: Once developed, any infrastructure must be able to evolve in order to accommodate changing student needs, technologies, and curricula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan for continuous change; build processes and structures that allow adaptation as curriculum, learning technologies, and approaches evolve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal vs real system deviations to anticipate
rubrics_metrics.description: An ideal online learning and teaching system is developed from scratch, with no restrictions on costs and staffing, and uninhibited by resistance to change. A real system will have deviations from the ideal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate and plan for limited resources; legacy systems with loyal advocates; key staff who must be retrained; unworkable policies and practices that require reinvention; inadequate governance processes; back-end administrative systems that may or may not be interfaceable; and an evolving understanding of pedagogical underpinnings. Design infrastructure and change-management strategies with these deviations in mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governance, change management, and LMS selection as strategic considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Without effective structures and processes, the selection, deployment, and ongoing performance of an online learning system will prove challenging and perhaps unsuccessful. Selection of and engagement with a single LMS (e.g., Moodle) can act as a catalyst in moving course creation, production, and delivery online.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address governance and change issues early; ensure effective decision-making processes, policies, and supports are in place to manage transitions. Recognize campus-based mixing of classroom and online learning and plan interfaces and services accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage distance education experience for quality and effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Distance education has provided an understanding of how the entire system of course design, development, and delivery occurs, and how these link to related learner services and other components, all of which are vital aspects of ensuring effectiveness and quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use established distance-education practices and lessons to inform online learning infrastructure, linking course design and delivery to learner services, production processes, and administrative systems to support quality.
